text: Vladimir Alexandrovich Voevodsky (/vɔɪɛˈvɒdski/, Russian: Влади́мир Алекса́ндрович Воево́дский; 4 June 1966 – 30 September 2017) was a Russian-American mathematician whose work in developing a homotopy theory for algebraic varieties and formulating motivic cohomology earned him the Fields Medal in 2002. He is also known for proving the Milnor conjecture and the motivic Bloch–Kato conjectures, as well as for pioneering the univalent foundations of mathematics and homotopy type theory. His father, Aleksander Voevodsky, was head of the Laboratory of High Energy Leptons at the Institute for Nuclear Research of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and his mother, Tatyana, was a chemist. Voevodsky attended Moscow State University but was expelled without a diploma for refusing to attend classes and failing academically. He received his Ph.D. in mathematics from Harvard University in 1992 after being recommended without applying or having a formal college degree, following several independent publications, and was advised by David Kazhdan. While a first-year undergraduate, he was given a copy of "Esquisse d'un Programme" by Alexander Grothendieck, which he learned in French solely to read, and began research on its themes. His work bridged algebraic geometry and algebraic topology; with Fabien Morel, he introduced a homotopy theory for schemes and formulated what is now considered the correct form of motivic cohomology, using it to prove Milnor's conjecture linking the Milnor K-theory of a field to its étale cohomology. For this, he was awarded the Fields Medal at the 24th International Congress of Mathematicians in Beijing, China. In 1998, he delivered a plenary lecture (A1-Homotopy Theory) at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Berlin. He coauthored with Andrei Suslin and Eric M. Friedlander the book Cycles, Transfers and Motivic Homology Theories, which details the theory of motivic cohomology. From 2002, he was a professor at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey. In January 2009, at a conference honoring Alexander Grothendieck at the Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques, Voevodsky announced a proof of the full Bloch–Kato conjectures. In 2009, he constructed the univalent model of Martin-Löf type theory in simplicial sets, leading to significant advances in type theory and the development of univalent foundations of mathematics, which he pursued in his final years. He worked on a Rocq (then: Coq) library called UniMath based on univalent ideas. In April 2016, the University of Gothenburg awarded him an honorary doctorate. Voevodsky died on 30 September 2017 at his home in Princeton, New Jersey, at the age of 51, from an aneurysm. He was survived by his daughters, Diana Yasmine Voevodsky and Natalia Dalia Shalaby.
